name: Fist bonesmashing

card.summary: Fist bonesmashing is the variant of bonesmashing in which the face is struck with the hands rather than a tool, with the aim, as proponents describe it, of triggering bone remodeling for a more defined jaw or cheekbones.
card.note: Surgeons warn of fractures, nerve and vascular injury, fat necrosis and permanent disfigurement; no published studies support the claimed benefit.

quick.overview:
Bonesmashing is an online looksmaxxing practice built on the idea that repeated trauma to facial bone will make it heal thicker and more prominent, giving a sharper jawline or cheekbones. The fist version refers to doing this with the hands instead of an object such as a hammer. Proponents invoke Wolff's law, the 19th-century idea that bone adapts to the loads placed on it.

Surgeons interviewed in news coverage say there is no scientific support for the approach and describe it as dangerous. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article describes bonesmashing as an inside joke that is rarely actually done, labelled misinformation in several sources.
quick.how: Descriptions in news coverage are general: people strike the cheek, jaw or brow area repeatedly in the belief that bone grows back stronger. The wiki does not describe methods. Some online discussion pairs the idea with other bone-related theories, including remodeling theories involving hormones.
quick.risks: Plastic surgeons warn of fractures, malalignment, nerve and blood-vessel injury, fat necrosis, bleeding that could affect the airway or vision, and permanent disfigurement. One surgeon notes healed bone typically regains only about 80% of its original strength. Medical centers recommend consulting a board-certified doctor about any facial change.

lead: Fist bonesmashing is a form of bonesmashing, a practice discussed on looksmaxxing forums and on TikTok in which people strike their own facial bones to try to reshape them. The "fist" label distinguishes hand strikes from the hammer or other tools that dominate news descriptions of the trend. Followers say the aim is a more chiselled jaw, cheekbone or brow.[1][2]

The rationale proponents give is Wolff's law, the 19th-century principle by German surgeon Julius Wolff that bone adapts to the stress placed on it. Those who attempt it, as described in news coverage, believe bone grows stronger as it heals.[2] Videos about bonesmashing have been reported to have more than 250 million views on TikTok.[2]

Plastic surgeons quoted in coverage say there is no scientific support for the idea. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says the practice is described as an inside joke that is rarely carried out and that sources call it misinformation, while noting doctors and facial surgeons warn of fractures, misalignment, nerve and blood-vessel injuries, deformity and vision changes.[1]

chain: Bone is said to remodel while healing
Claimed: thicker, sharper jaw or cheekbones
angle.text: Proponents say healing bone grows back stronger and more prominent under Wolff's law, giving sharper contours without surgery. Surgeons dispute this and describe injury as the likely outcome.

infobox: Hands/fists, as opposed to a hammer or tool

paras: Bonesmashing gained wide attention in 2023 and 2024 through coverage in outlets including Vice, CBS Baltimore, the Daily Dot, Esquire and The Guardian, as listed in Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article, which describes it as hitting the face with objects such as hammers for a chiselled look.[1] The fist variant appears in discussion as the hand-based version of the same idea.

Practitioners cite Wolff's law and the idea that bones thicken as they heal.[2] Coverage connected the trend to the influencer Clavicular, who is reported to claim that bonesmashing causes minor damage after which bones heal with greater facial harmony.[1]

Dr. Ben Schultz, a plastic and reconstructive surgeon at LifeBridge Health, told CBS Baltimore the practice is not backed by science. He said healed bone typically regains about 80% of original strength, that the face's many blood vessels mean bleeding could threaten the airway or vision, and that nerve damage is possible. He also noted that the bony outgrowths practitioners seek, osteophytes, are growths beyond normal limits.[2]

Dr. Christine Stiles of UT Southwestern calls it one of the most concerning looksmaxxing practices, saying repeated blows can damage skin and subcutaneous tissue, cause fat necrosis and injure the bone, leaving a permanently disfigured face and starting a cycle of corrective procedures.[3]

timeline.event: News coverage of bonesmashing appears in Vice, CBS Baltimore, the Daily Dot and others.[1]
The Guardian covers bonesmashing and chin extensions.[1]

lore.intro: Online, bonesmashing is discussed as a theory about bone remodeling, while many observers describe it as a joke or as misinformation.[1]

claims.claim: Striking facial bone makes it heal thicker and more prominent
claims.believers: Proponents cite Wolff's law and say bone grows stronger as it heals.[2]
claims.experts: Surgeons say the practice is not backed by science and that healed bone regains only part of its strength.[2]

claims.claim: Self-inflicted impacts are safe if the damage is minor
claims.believers: Coverage attributes to one influencer the claim that bonesmashing causes only minor damage.[1]
claims.experts: Surgeons describe risks of fractures, nerve and vessel injury, fat necrosis and disfigurement.[2][3]
